title: AI Is Transforming Incident Response - but the Hardest Problems May Still Belong to Humans
gist: A discussion from Uptime Labs' Incident Fest, with input from Chime and Rootly, argues AI in incident response creates a paradox: automating routine failures leaves humans only the rare, ambiguous, high-consequence incidents while stripping away the practice that builds the skill to handle them. Research cited by J. Paul Reed shows correct AI recommendations lift human performance substantially but incorrect ones degrade it below the no-AI baseline, and NIST's 2026 work flags unresolved gaps in human-AI feedback loops — meanwhile AI-generated code raises change volume, the primary driver of incident frequency.

themes.theme: The automation paradox in incident response

insights.claim: The more routine incident work AI automates, the more important human expertise becomes for failures that are novel, complex or unexpected — a paradox rather than a straight substitution.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Headcount-reduction theses for SRE built on AI ops tooling are likely to be wrong on the senior end of the skill curve.
insights.quote: the more routine work AI automates, the more important human expertise becomes when systems fail in ways that are novel, complex, or unexpected
insights.locator: But according to a recent discussion highlighted by Uptime Labs

insights.claim: The argument is not to reject AI in the incident command center but to be deliberate about introducing it, because automation can erode the skills, situational awareness and decision-making needed when the AI hits its limits.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Deliberate rollout design, not tool selection, is where operational risk is created or avoided in AI ops adoption.
insights.locator: The discussion brings together perspectives from Uptime Labs, Chime, and Rootly

insights.claim: The Leftover Principle holds that as automation absorbs routine tasks, the residual human workload consists disproportionately of the unusual, ambiguous and difficult problems automation could not solve.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A transferable model for any function being partly automated: the average task gets easier while the marginal task gets harder, which changes hiring and training economics.
insights.locator: One of the most compelling ideas raised in the discussion is the Leftover Principle

insights.claim: The concept echoes decades of research into the ironies of automation, in which automating more inadvertently weakens the human capabilities needed precisely when automation fails.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A well-established failure mode from aviation and process control is now arriving in software operations, so the mitigations are already known.
insights.locator: The concept echoes decades of research into the ironies of automation

themes.theme: AI recommendation quality cuts both ways

insights.claim: Research discussed by J. Paul Reed indicates that when AI diagnostic recommendations are correct, human responders perform substantially better than without AI assistance.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: The upside case for AI-assisted diagnosis is empirically supported, which is why adoption will continue regardless of the skill-atrophy critique.
insights.locator: Uptime Labs cites research discussed by J. Paul Reed

insights.claim: The same research shows misleading AI assistance can significantly degrade human performance relative to working with no AI at all, making recommendation accuracy a two-sided risk rather than a one-sided benefit.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Expected-value math for AI ops tools must weight the downside of wrong answers, not just the average accuracy figure vendors quote.
insights.locator: the same research highlights the danger of incorrect recommendations

insights.claim: The operative lesson is not to 'use AI' but to establish when its output can be trusted, how it should be challenged and when humans must take back control.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Trust calibration procedures are the emerging operational requirement — and a product gap current AI ops tools mostly do not fill.
insights.locator: The lesson is therefore not simply to "use AI"

themes.theme: Skill atrophy and the accountability gap

insights.claim: If AI handles straightforward failures, engineers encounter fewer routine incidents and get less practice, so the people facing an exceptionally complex failure will have less hands-on experience than previous generations.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Reliability risk shifts from mean-time-to-repair on common incidents toward catastrophic tail incidents handled by less-practiced staff.
insights.locator: Incident response is particularly vulnerable to this effect

insights.claim: Responders may lose situational context because they enter an incident only after the AI has already performed much of the initial investigation, arriving without the understanding that investigation would have built.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Handoff design between agent and human is a specific, testable failure point in every AI-assisted ops deployment.

insights.claim: Organizations risk an accountability gap in which humans remain responsible for decisions without retaining the expertise to make them confidently.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Liability sits with humans while competence migrates to systems — a governance exposure regulated industries will have to answer for.
insights.locator: organizations may create an accountability gap

insights.claim: Maintaining responder skill requires deliberate investment in game days, simulations, tabletop exercises, chaos engineering and regular incident-response practice, since real incidents no longer supply enough reps.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Synthetic practice becomes a budget line rather than an optional exercise — a demand driver for chaos-engineering and incident-simulation vendors.
insights.locator: they may need to invest more deliberately in maintaining those skills

insights.claim: NIST's 2026 research into monitoring deployed AI systems flags insufficient study of human-AI feedback loops, the difficulty of scaling human-driven monitoring alongside rapid AI deployment, and the unresolved balance between automated and human-validated monitoring.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A standards body naming these gaps is an early marker of future compliance requirements around AI-in-the-loop operations.
insights.locator: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has also identified

insights.claim: Simply placing a human somewhere in an AI-driven process is not sufficient; organizations must understand how humans interact with AI recommendations and how those interactions affect decision quality over time.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Nominal human-in-the-loop compliance is not a real control, which undercuts a common assurance claim in AI governance documents.
insights.locator: These findings reinforce the idea that simply placing a human

themes.theme: Change volume as the incident driver

insights.claim: Incident frequency is a product of two variables — the volume of changes and the probability that any individual change introduces a failure — and AI-assisted development can raise the first substantially.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A simple model for forecasting incident load in AI-accelerated engineering orgs, and for arguing reliability budget.
insights.quote: the number of incidents is influenced by both the volume of changes and the probability that any individual change introduces a failure
insights.locator: The Uptime Labs discussion frames incident frequency in simple terms

insights.claim: Whether AI raises or lowers overall incident counts depends on the quality of AI-generated code, tests, dependencies and configurations, which determines the per-change failure probability.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: The key empirical question for reliability in 2026 is per-change defect rate of agent-authored code — track it before assuming either outcome.
insights.locator: AI could increase the first variable substantially

insights.claim: Accelerating change makes established engineering practices more important, not less: deployment controls, observability, feature flags, automated testing, resilience engineering and rapid rollback become critical safeguards.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Delivery-safety tooling is a direct beneficiary of AI coding adoption — a durable demand thesis for that software category.
insights.locator: This makes established engineering practices more important, not less

insights.claim: The objective should not be preventing every AI-generated mistake but ensuring mistakes are detected quickly, contained effectively and reversed safely.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Containment-over-prevention reframes where engineering investment should go when defect volume rises faster than review capacity.
insights.quote: The objective should not necessarily be to prevent every AI-generated mistake, but to ensure that mistakes are detected quickly, contained effectively, and reversed safely.
insights.locator: The objective should not necessarily be to prevent

insights.claim: AI could fundamentally change the incident responder's role — toward rare, ambiguous, high-consequence failures beyond automated diagnosis — without eliminating the need for incident responders.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Expect role redefinition and premium pay for deep-expertise responders rather than shrinkage of the on-call function.
insights.quote: AI could fundamentally change the role of the incident responder without eliminating the need for incident responders themselves.
insights.locator: The most important takeaway from Uptime Labs' discussion
